caption:
Why were Hagia Sophia's mosaics covered up?

Justinian I finished the church in 537. On seeing it he is said to have declared: "Solomon, I have surpassed thee."

Constantinople fell in 1453 and Mehmed II ordered the church converted into a mosque the day he entered it. Under Suleiman the Magnificent, the mosaics of Jesus, Mary and the Byzantine emperors above the narthex and imperial gates were covered with whitewash and plaster.

The plaster is why they survived. Mosque workers were selling mosaic cubes to visitors as talismans; when Ahmed III had the crumbling plaster renewed in 1717, it shielded the images underneath. The white plaster came off in 1930, and the building opened as a museum in 1935.

The 1847–49 restoration by Gaspare and Giuseppe Fossati had already exposed and cleaned the upper gallery mosaics — then covered many of them again "for protection against further damage". Their sketches record what they saw.

Still open: in 2020 the museum decision was annulled and Hagia Sophia became a mosque again. The apse mosaics of the Virgin and Child were hung with white drapes for the first Friday prayers. UNESCO has expressed grave concern about the state of conservation. In February 2026, seven Byzantine tunnel lines roughly 1,600 years old were documented beneath the building for the first time.

Images: an 1890s exterior from an album by the Abdullah frères and Zangaki; Gaspare Fossati's 1852 nave lithograph with Louis Haghe; the Fossati brothers' sketch of the mosaics they found; and photographs of the Zoe, Deesis and southwestern entrance mosaics by Myrabella. All public domain.

cards.note: Under Suleiman the Magnificent, mosaics of Jesus, Mary and emperors were plastered over. They were uncovered in 1930.

cards.source: Gaspare Fossati, lithograph by Louis Haghe, 1852

cards.headline: Two brothers <y>drew what they uncovered</y>, then hid it again
cards.note: The Fossati brothers recorded mosaics found in the eastern arch and apse. Many were then covered again for protection.
cards.source: Gaspare and Giuseppe Fossati, 1847–49 · public domain
cards.alt: Watercolour sketch of an enthroned Virgin in blue holding a standing child figure.

cards.headline: <y>11th-century gold</y>: Christ between an emperor and Zoe
cards.note: Christ Pantocrator with Constantine IX Monomachos and the Empress Zoe. Greek lettering names them both.
cards.source: Empress Zoe mosaic, 11th c. · photo Myrabella
cards.alt: Gold mosaic of Christ enthroned holding a book, a crowned empress standing at right.

cards.headline: Of the <y>Deesis mosaic</y>, only the upper part survives
cards.note: A 13th-century work. Below the three faces the wall is bare plaster, with a few stray tesserae left.
cards.alt: Damaged gold mosaic: Christ centre, a veiled figure left, a bearded figure right.

cards.headline: Uncovered in 1930 — the apse Virgin was <y>draped again in 2020</y>
cards.note: Turkey says the Christian images remain protected. UNESCO has asked for reports and expressed grave concern.
